title: Rural Vet Call Logs as Outbreak Early Warning
one_liner: Producers call the vet before they call the state. Anonymized weekly counts of abortions, maggot wounds, sudden deaths and respiratory clusters are a leading indicator that traders, insurers and packers will pay for.
customer: Buyers: cattle and feeder analytics desks, market advisory and commodity funds, packer and feedlot risk managers, livestock and dairy insurers or reinsurers, animal health company territory teams, and state animal health boards (contracts or grants). Suppliers are participating rural vets, who get free early regional alerts and a small revenue share.
problem: Official disease data lags by weeks because it waits on lab confirmation, and ranchers hesitate to report to the state because a quarantine costs them money. Screwworm was confirmed in a Texas calf in June 2026 after roughly 60 years without a US case, and H5N1 in dairy cattle was spreading for months before detection in 2024. Cattle futures at record prices with a 70-year low herd move violently on rumor, and nobody has a systematic ground-level feed.
solution: A 30-second end-of-week SMS or one-tap tally where each vet reports counts by syndrome (abortion clusters, navel or wound maggots, sudden deaths, neurological, respiratory, milk drops) and ZIP3 or county. Counts are aggregated with k-anonymity (no client identity, minimum practice thresholds) and compared to seasonal baselines. Outputs are a weekly 'Rural Vet Pulse' regional index, push alerts when a region deviates, and an API for institutional subscribers. Vets get the regional alerts free, which is the give-to-get hook.
why_now: New World screwworm has been confirmed in Texas and New Mexico since June 2026, with the first infested horse reported in September 2026, and movement restrictions plus sterile-fly shortages make the outbreak's trajectory the biggest driver of cattle risk. H5N1 in dairy is ongoing, federal animal health staffing is stretched, and academic syndromic surveillance systems exist in Europe (Netherlands, France, Great Britain) but I found no commercial equivalent built from US rural vet practices.
revenue_model: $2-10K per month per institutional data subscriber (analytics desks, insurers, packers), enterprise API tiers, sponsored regional alerts from animal health companies, state or regional government pilots, and a $100-300 per month revenue share to each contributing practice.
non_obvious_insight: Ranchers under-report to the state because reporting costs them money, but they do not hide problems from their vet because they need the vet's drugs and help. The vet's phone is the earliest sensor in the system, and vets cannot share client data but can share counts. Contrarian point: the absence of calls is also a signal, because call volume drops when producers hide problems during a quarantine.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 large-animal practices in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Kansas and Nebraska through state VMA lists and large-animal vet Facebook groups. Build the weekly tally as a plain SMS survey, with no software integration. Publish a free regional weekly newsletter to the vets as the hook. Backtest screwworm lead time against USDA confirmation dates and pitch 3 market-advisory or cattle analytics shops for a $1-2K per month paid pilot.
